description: We are Physics and Computer Science & Engineering students interested in astronomy, data analysis, and visualization. We aim to build a user-friendly web prototype that makes SPHEREx data easier to access, explore, and understand through interactive visualizations. We're excited to make astronomy informative and fun! We're looking for teammates with skills in web development, UI/UX design, Python, data science, and astronomy.
summary:
Our project aims to develop a user-friendly, interactive website that makes astronomical data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission more accessible to everyone. Users can enter a celestial object's coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), and the website searches multiple SPHEREx observations of that region to help identify and compare objects across images. Once an object is identified, the platform provides a simple introduction to what it might be, such as a star, gas cloud, or nebula, along with informative details about its characteristics. By comparing observations taken at different times, users can explore how objects and their surroundings change, including possible movement or variations in brightness.

The project addresses the challenge of making large astronomical datasets easier for the public to understand and explore. Rather than requiring users to have an astronomy background or interpret raw scientific data themselves, our website aims to turn complex observations into an approachable learning experience. We believe this is important because it can spark curiosity about space, encourage scientific exploration, and help people connect with real data collected by a space telescope.
details:
Sky Movie Player(SMP) is an interactive website designed to make astronomical observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission more accessible and understandable to the public.

The website is designed to allow users to enter the Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates of a region in the sky and explore observations of that region taken at different times. By comparing multiple images, users can identify objects that appear in both observations, investigate possible movement, and explore changes in brightness. The platform also aims to provide simple explanations and information about identified celestial objects, such as stars, brown dwarfs, and other astronomical sources.

How It Works:

Our team began by developing the basic frontend and backend structure of the website. We also created a separate Python-based Object Finder prototype to experiment with astronomical image comparison. Using two programmatically generated sample images representing the same region of space, our code detects matching objects and highlights objects that appear in only one image. This allowed us to test the fundamental image-comparison process.

Our original approach was to develop smaller tools independently, including object finding, image retrieval, image alignment, and object identification, before integrating them into one platform. We established the initial website and image-comparison prototype, while integration with real SPHEREx observations remains a future development goal.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project aims to reduce the complexity of exploring astronomical datasets by presenting observations through an accessible and interactive interface. It can encourage public participation in scientific exploration, help beginners understand changes in the night sky, and make space science more engaging for people without specialized astronomy knowledge.

Tools and Technologies:

  • HTML: Structuring the website's content and interface.
  • Python: Image comparison and object-matching experiments.
  • NumPy and image-processing libraries: Processing and comparing sample images.
  • Frontend development: Building the website interface.
  • Backend development: Establishing the website's underlying structure.
  • NASA/IPAC SPHEREx Archive (IRSA): Identified as the intended source for future real-data integration.

Our approach focuses on breaking a complex astronomical analysis process into smaller, manageable tools that can eventually work together within one website. We considered accessibility for beginners, ease of navigation, coordinate-based searching, image comparison, and the challenges of handling large astronomical datasets. We also used generated sample images to experiment with our image-matching approach before connecting it to real telescope observations.

Our long-term vision is to create a beginner-friendly platform that turns complex space observations into an interactive experience, helping more people explore and appreciate the discoveries hidden in astronomical data.
